Out of the blue today, I got an email offering help with my Vis-MLM book. Not a review, not a
question about the content -- a pitch. "Quick question," it began. "I came across Vis-MLM-book
today and ended up reading through the whole thing. Has anyone ever looked at it from the outside
and told you what they noticed first?"

It went on like that for a few paragraphs: a folksy theory about five-second first impressions, my
repo's 21 GitHub stars offered up as proof that "not enough of the right people are getting past
those five seconds," and a free offer to send me a plan for fixing my README. "I am not trying to
sell you anything in this email," it assured me, which is the kind of sentence that only shows up
in emails that are, in fact, building up to selling you something.

The sender's address was `bodassss3456@gmail.com`. Not a company. Not even a plausible person.
Just a handle with the specific gravity of a bulk-mail template behind it.

### Sicking my agent on their agent

Vis-MLM-book is a Quarto repo for a book manuscript I'm writing with Claude Code's help --
which meant that, when this landed, I had an AI assistant sitting right there. So I did the
obvious, slightly juvenile thing: I asked Claude to read the pitch and tell me what it thought,
then draft a reply. My agent versus -- presumably -- theirs.

It didn't take much prompting. Claude clocked the email as templated outreach almost immediately:
the "quick question" opener, the manufactured personalization (a star count is not an insight),
the pre-emptive "I'm not selling anything." I asked for something blunt, and got back a genuinely
well-constructed dismissal -- something like:

> No.
>
> This is a form email... My assistant flagged it as templated outreach in about two seconds,
> which is roughly the "five seconds" you claim decides whether something's worth attention...
> Please don't darken my inbox again.

<!-- TODO: decide whether to quote the reply in full here, or just this flavor excerpt -->

It was sharp. It was fun to read. I was, for about thirty seconds, ready to send it.

### The swerve

Then I asked Claude one more question before hitting send: was there anything about this account
that should worry me enough to just let it go?

The answer was the actual point of this whole exercise, and it wasn't the one I expected. The
email itself was harmless -- no link, no attachment, nothing to click. But replying, even with a
witty takedown, does something the spammer wants: it confirms the mailbox is real, live, and
read by a human who responds to cold outreach. That's valuable information, and it's the kind of
thing that gets sold, reused, and acted on -- more outreach, not less. A clever rebuttal doesn't
punish a bulk-mail operation. It feeds it a signal.

So the reply I was proud of is the reply that never got sent. I marked the email as junk in
Outlook instead, and it vanished immediately -- no confirmation screen, no "are you sure," just
gone. Oddly satisfying, in a way that a perfect comeback never would have been.

### Who actually won

There's something a little absurd about setting up a "battle of the agents" and then having the
battle consist of my agent talking me out of fighting. But I think that's the real shape of this
particular fight: against automated, at-scale outreach, the winning move isn't a better sword,
it's not showing up to the duel. My assistant didn't beat theirs by writing something clever. It
won by telling me the clever thing wasn't worth using.

Which leaves an odd question hanging over the whole exercise: what does it even mean to win a
fight the other side never knew happened?
